early_history_summary: Thomas Gleixner is a German Linux kernel developer best known for real-time Linux work and core kernel maintenance (timers/irq/x86). He started a Linux-for-industry business in 1996 (later Linutronix), increased kernel contributions from around 2000, and became a key figure in the PREEMPT_RT effort.
evidence_summary: Gleixner has no English Wikipedia biography and no published birth year in sources reviewed (Linux Foundation interviews, Linutronix materials, kernel maintainer profiles). name: Mislav Marohnić
category: Open-source engineer / GitHub CLI and Ruby tooling
milestone_by_age_26: By about 2007 (age ~21) he was already the primary author/maintainer of will_paginate, a widely adopted Rails pagination library, and by ~2010 (age ~24) he created and began long-term maintenance of hub, the popular GitHub-oriented git CLI wrapper.
early_history_summary: Mislav Marohnić is a Croatian software engineer who became a prominent open-source contributor in the Ruby/Rails community. He authored will_paginate (with early co-credit to PJ Hyett), later created hub, and worked as an engineer at GitHub while living as a remote/traveling developer from Zagreb and elsewhere.
family_context_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. He is from Croatia (Zagreb area associations).
primary_early_advantage_tags: Rails ecosystem, GitHub, will_paginate, hub, open source, Croatia remote work
evidence_summary: Batch data and self-description as an '80s kid support a ~1986 birth year. By the mid/late 2000s he shipped will_paginate into the core Rails toolbox and then built hub, which he maintained for a decade-plus and which became a defining GitHub CLI tool before official gh. Early advantages were primarily platform-native: deep Rails/GitHub open-source distribution and collaboration (including with PJ Hyett), not documented family capital or elite institutions.
starting_point: From Croatia (Zagreb associations); family class and parental occupations not documented in reviewed sources.
current_position: Independent open-source engineer known for hub and will_paginate; formerly a GitHub engineer; continues open-source work and writing from a remote/traveling base.

trajectory.event: will_paginate was already in active Rails community use as his major pagination library contribution.
Created hub and began long-term maintenance of the GitHub-oriented git CLI wrapper.
Active in the Zagreb developer community while building a remote open-source/GitHub career.
Published a retrospective on a decade of hub maintenance as GitHub's official gh CLI matured.

name: Jacob Abraham
category: Computer scientist / VLSI testing and fault-tolerant computing
milestone_by_age_26: Completed a Ph.D. in electrical engineering and computer science at Stanford University in 1974 at age 25 under Edward J. McCluskey, after an M.S. from Stanford in 1971, then joined the University of Illinois faculty in 1975 at age 26.
early_history_summary: Born in Kerala, India on December 8, 1948, Abraham earned a B.E. in electrical engineering from the University of Kerala in 1970, then an M.S. (1971) and Ph.D. (1974) at Stanford under Edward J. McCluskey. He joined the University of Illinois faculty in 1975 and later moved to UT Austin (1988), building a major research program in VLSI test, formal verification, and fault-tolerant computing.
family_context_summary: Born in Kerala, India; early family financial and educational context not detailed in reviewed sources.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Stanford, McCluskey, University of Illinois, VLSI test, fault tolerance
evidence_summary: Abraham moved rapidly from a University of Kerala bachelor's (1970) through Stanford M.S. and Ph.D. (1971, 1974) under leading testing researcher Edward J. McCluskey, then onto the Illinois faculty in 1975 at age 26. Early advantage was primarily institutional: elite graduate training and mentorship at Stanford during the formative era of digital testing research, not documented family wealth or industry inheritance. Later career awards (IEEE Piore, ACM/IEEE Fellow) confirmed long-run impact.
starting_point: Born December 8, 1948 in Kerala, India; undergraduate training at University of Kerala; family occupations not documented.
current_position: Professor emeritus and Cockrell Family Regents Chair in Engineering at UT Austin ECE; director of the Computer Engineering Research Center; IEEE and ACM Fellow.

trajectory.event: Received bachelor's degree in electrical engineering from the University of Kerala.
Completed M.S. in electrical engineering at Stanford University.
Completed Ph.D. in EE/CS at Stanford under Edward J. McCluskey.
Joined the faculty of the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign.
Moved to the University of Texas at Austin as a faculty member.
Received the IEEE Emanuel R. Piore Award for contributions to VLSI testing and fault-tolerant computing.

name: Kevin Cloud
milestone_by_age_26: Born 1965 (month unknown). First full-time computer-artist job at Softdisk in 1985 (~age 20) is employment rather than a breakout success; hired by id Software on March 10, 1992 at age 26 or 27 depending on birth month; Doom (Dec 1993) arrived at ~age 28. No firm material milestone firmly dated at age ≤26.
early_history_summary: Kevin Cloud grew up in Shreveport, Louisiana, graduated LSU-Shreveport in 1987 with a political science degree, and worked as a computer artist and illustrator at Softdisk (including Loadstar) from about 1985. He joined id Software in 1992 as assistant artist to Adrian Carmack, worked on Wolfenstein 3D, Doom, Quake and later titles, became a co-owner until the ZeniMax deal, and later served as senior producer before retiring around late 2023.
family_context_summary: Born in 1965 to a teacher and an electrician; grew up in Shreveport reading comics and playing arcades (MobyGames biography).
parent_family_domain_summary: Parents were a teacher and an electrician; no documented game-industry domain transfer.
evidence_summary: Multiple secondary sources give birth year 1965, and Wikipedia/Gamasutra document the March 10, 1992 id hire and Doom-era art credit. Because birth month is unknown, age at the id hire may be 27; the defining public success (Doom, Dec 1993) was at about age 28. Conservatively treated as age_26_ineligible.

name: Gloria Bolotsky
milestone_by_age_26: By 1946 (age 24–25) she was programming the ENIAC at the University of Pennsylvania as part of the early scientific programming team (famously photographed for Life magazine), then in 1947 (age 25–26) joined a secret computing group at Aberdeen Proving Ground.
early_history_summary: Gloria Ruth Gordon was born in New York City on July 28, 1921, studied nursing briefly, then earned a mathematics degree from Brooklyn College. She worked as a mathematician at the Brooklyn Navy Yard before moving to Philadelphia to help program ENIAC, later worked at Aberdeen Proving Ground, taught high-school math briefly, and spent ~20 years at the National Bureau of Standards on networking and ADP systems.
family_context_summary: Born in New York City; later married metallurgist Max Bolotsky in 1948 and raised five daughters in Rockville, Maryland. Childhood family finances not detailed in reviewed sources.
primary_early_advantage_tags: ENIAC, wartime computing, Brooklyn College math, Aberdeen Proving Ground, women in early programming
evidence_summary: Bolotsky entered electronic computing at its birth: math training plus wartime demand placed her on the ENIAC programming effort by her mid-20s, with physical access to the first general-purpose electronic computer and a large peer cohort of early programmers. Family domain advantage is undocumented; the decisive stack was institutional wartime computing opportunity and scarce machine access rather than inherited capital. Later NBS career extended her work into networking and federal ADP systems.
starting_point: Born July 28, 1921 in New York City; studied nursing then mathematics at Brooklyn College; early family occupations not documented.
current_position: Died June 30, 2009 in Gaithersburg, Maryland at age 87; final long career phase was ~20 years at the U.S. National Bureau of Standards on networking and ADP systems.

trajectory.event: Worked on ENIAC programming at the University of Pennsylvania; appeared (uncredited at the time) in a Life magazine photograph of the machine.
Joined a secret computing group at Aberdeen Proving Ground in Maryland.
Married metallurgist Max Bolotsky and continued a technical career while raising a family.
Joined the National Bureau of Standards in Gaithersburg, beginning a ~20-year federal computing career.
Died of cancer in Gaithersburg, Maryland.

name: Len Bass
milestone_by_age_26: Born c.1943. Graduated with a bachelor's in mathematics in California in 1964 (~age 21) and received a Ph.D. in computer science from Purdue in 1970 (~age 27), then became a professor at the University of Rhode Island. Software-architecture fame (SEI books) came decades later; no material milestone firmly at age ≤26 found.
early_history_summary: Leonard Joel (Len) Bass is known for software architecture practice through long tenure at Carnegie Mellon's Software Engineering Institute and co-authorship of Software Architecture in Practice. He earned a Purdue Ph.D. in 1970, taught at URI, joined SEI in 1986, later worked at NICTA, and has taught DevOps/architecture courses as CMU adjunct faculty.
evidence_summary: Wikipedia gives birth year c.1943 and Ph.D. year 1970 (~age 27). His defining contributions to software architecture practice are associated with SEI work beginning in 1986, well after age 26.

name: Alexia Tsotsis
milestone_by_age_26: Born 1982. Worked in New York media and at LA Weekly/SF Weekly in her 20s; joined TechCrunch in 2010 at age ~28, made Forbes 30 Under 30 Media in 2011 (~age 29), and became TechCrunch co-editor in February 2012 (~age 29–30). No material milestone by age 26 found.
early_history_summary: Alexia Bonatsos (née Tsotsis) studied at USC, spent years trying to break into media in New York (with side classes at NYU), wrote for LA Weekly and SF Weekly, then rose at TechCrunch to co-editor. She later completed Stanford MSx, founded venture firm Dream Machine, and is a general partner investing in technology startups.
evidence_summary: Wikipedia and contemporary TechCrunch/Forbes coverage place her TechCrunch hire in 2010 and co-editorship in 2012, both after age 26 given a 1982 birth year. Earlier alt-weekly work is pre-breakout rather than a dated material milestone for this dataset.

name: Parisa Tabriz
milestone_by_age_26: Co-authored a USENIX Security Symposium paper on 802.11 device driver fingerprinting in 2006 at about age 23, then joined Google's security team as an information security engineer in 2007 at about age 24 after B.S./M.S. degrees at UIUC.
early_history_summary: Parisa Tabriz was born in 1983 in Chicago to an Iranian physician father and Polish-American nurse mother. She studied computer science at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign (B.S. and M.S.), did wireless security research with Nikita Borisov, interned at Google security, and joined Google full-time in 2007. She later led Chrome security, Project Zero, and rose to VP/GM of Chrome.
family_context_summary: Born in Chicago suburbs to an Iranian immigrant father who was a doctor and a Polish-American mother who was a nurse; older sister of two brothers.
parent_family_domain_summary: Parents worked in medicine/nursing rather than computing; no documented computer-security domain transfer from family.
primary_early_advantage_tags: UIUC CS, Nikita Borisov, USENIX Security, Google security, Chrome, professional family
evidence_summary: Tabriz entered security research as a student (club after her site was hacked; papers with Borisov including USENIX Security 2006) and converted that into a Google security hire in 2007 at ~24. Early advantages were strong but conventional for elite CS: professional-class family resources, UIUC research pipeline, and immersion in Google's security org during the rise of large-scale web security—not inherited industry status. Later public fame as 'Security Princess,' Chrome security lead (2013), Project Zero (2016), and Chrome VP came after age 26.
starting_point: Born 1983 in Chicago suburbs to an Iranian doctor father and Polish-American nurse mother; older of three siblings.
current_position: Vice President and General Manager of Google Chrome; also associated with Project Zero leadership history; known as Google's 'Security Princess'.

trajectory.event: Co-authored a USENIX Security paper on passive 802.11 wireless device driver fingerprinting.
Joined Google's security team as an information security engineer after completing UIUC degrees.
Took over responsibility for Google Chrome security and drove HTTPS adoption efforts.
Assumed responsibility for Google Project Zero.
Became head of Product and Engineering for Google Chrome.
Served as Vice President of the Chrome division at Google.
